subject: english-language-and-literature
title: English Language and Literature MYP 5 eAssessment Structure Mock B (7 tasks, 80 marks)

questions.content:
[[Q 1.1 | A 2]]
Task 1: Analysing
Questions 1.1 to 1.4 focus on the key concept of communication. Question 1.5 focuses on the key concept of connections. The criteria assessed are A (Analysing) and B (Organizing). Suggested time for Questions 1.1 to 1.4: 15 minutes. Suggested time for Question 1.5: 35 minutes.

Text A: 'Night Mode' (an extract from a short story, written for this paper)
This extract describes Kofi, a fifteen-year-old, awake in his bedroom in the early hours of a school night.

At 1.17 a.m. the phone lit Kofi's face from below, which made him look, he thought, like someone telling a ghost story to himself. He was not asleep. He had stopped pretending to be around midnight, when the tenth video in a row about a stranger's perfect morning had slid into the eleventh without his thumb ever deciding anything.

The screen gave nothing back. That was its gift and its crime. It never grew tired, never said enough, never looked at him with the particular patience of his father at the kitchen table. It simply refreshed, and a new face appeared, laughing at a joke he had missed.

Somewhere below his window a bin lorry groaned, and the ordinary noise startled him: a real thing, made by real people on a real night shift. He looked up. His bedroom had been there all along: the poster peeling at one corner, the chemistry homework glowing faintly white on the desk like a small accusation, the dark square of the window.

The phone buzzed in his hand.

Mara: you up?

Two words. He typed an answer, deleted it, typed another. Every version looked like a boy pretending not to care. In the end he did what he always did. He sent a thumbs-up, a small yellow hand lifted in the dark, and the conversation ended where it had begun.

Mara had been his best friend since they were seven. Mara lived four streets away. They sat in the same row in registration, and in six weeks neither had said a sentence to the other that was longer than a reaction.

He lay back. The ceiling had a crack in it shaped like a river. For a second he imagined pulling on his trainers, walking the four streets, and throwing a pebble at her window. Four streets was nothing. It had somehow become the longest distance he knew.

He turned the phone face down on the duvet. The room did not collapse. The light drained from his hands, and the darkness came up around him, soft and enormous and slightly frightening, like the deep end when you first let go of the side.

Text B: poster for 'The Look Up Challenge' (written for this paper; in the live exam this would be an image)

[Layout: a tall poster with a dark navy background. The top two-thirds is a photograph of a crowded bus stop at dusk. Six people stand in a row and every head is bowed over a glowing phone, their faces lit a pale, ghostly blue. The whole photograph is in muted blue-grey, with one exception. At the far right edge a small girl in a yellow raincoat looks straight out at the viewer, and in her hand is a bright red paper kite.]

[Across the middle of the poster, in huge white capitals:] WHO ARE YOU MISSING?

[Beneath it, in smaller gold type:] Our survey of 2,000 teenagers found that most check their phones more than eighty times a day. How many times did you look up?

[Centred body text in white, in short lines, with generous space between them:]
Your friends are not in your pocket.
They are at the next bus stop.
The next table.
The next street.

[A row of three small white icons, each with a one-word caption underneath: a phone lying face down, "PARK IT"; two speech bubbles, "SAY IT"; a sunrise over a hill, "GO OUTSIDE".]

Seven days. One rule. When you are with people, phones go face down.

[Across the bottom, a bright red band with white capitals:] START MONDAY. TELL THREE FRIENDS. #LOOKUP

[Small print in the bottom corner:] A project of the Greenfield Youth Trust. Join in at lookupchallenge.example. No apps. No downloads. Just people.

Q 1.1 Comment on the use of light in the first two paragraphs of Text A. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 2 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies a use of light with a reference to the text but does not explain its effect, e.g. the phone 'lit Kofi's face from below'. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): comments on the use of light with an example and some explanation, e.g. the cold glow of the phone from below, compared to a ghost-story teller, makes Kofi seem eerie and cut off, and suggests the screen is the only source of life in his night; the screen 'gave nothing back' as light without warmth. [1] Accept any valid effect, for example isolation, unreality or the unnatural hour. Award 0 for no or incorrect reference to the text.

questions.content:
[[Q 1.2 | A 3]]
Refer to Text A (printed in Question 1.1). Explain the effect of the lines: 'Four streets was nothing. It had somehow become the longest distance he knew.' (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 3 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies an effect without developing it, e.g. it shows Kofi is far from his friend. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes an effect with some example or explanation, e.g. the contrast between 'nothing' and 'the longest distance' shows that physical closeness has been replaced by emotional distance. [1] Level 3 (3 marks): explains the effect consistently with well-chosen quotation, e.g. the very short first sentence mirrors how easy the walk would be, then the longer second sentence with the reflective 'somehow' conveys Kofi's confusion and sadness; the paradox implies that constant digital contact has made real contact harder, so the reader feels the loss of the friendship. [1] Accept any valid reading supported by the text.

questions.content:
[[Q 1.3 | A 2]]
Refer to Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Describe the purpose of the colour in the photograph. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 2 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies a purpose without explanation, e.g. the colours make the people look dull. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes the purpose with an example or explanation, e.g. the muted blue-grey of the phone users makes them look cold and lifeless, while the bright red kite and the yellow raincoat of the girl draw the eye and suggest that real life, play and connection are vivid and are found by looking up. [1] Accept: to contrast absorption in screens with the energy of the real world; to focus on the girl as the model of behaviour.

questions.content:
[[Q 1.4 | A 3]]
Refer to Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Analyse the effect of a technique used in Text B. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 3 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies a technique and an effect with no development, e.g. the poster uses a question as the headline. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes the effect of one technique with some justification, e.g. the question 'WHO ARE YOU MISSING?' addresses the viewer directly and makes them feel slightly guilty, so they keep reading. [1] Level 3 (3 marks): analyses the effect consistently with a precise example, e.g. the list structure 'The next bus stop. The next table. The next street.' uses repetition and a falling rhythm to move from the public to the personal, so that friends seem close enough to reach; the red band with imperatives 'START MONDAY. TELL THREE FRIENDS.' turns guilt into a simple action. [1] Accept any valid technique: statistics, imagery, imperative verbs, hashtag, icons, small print 'No apps. Just people.', layout.

questions.content:
[[Q 1.5 | A 10 | B 10]]
Refer to Text A and Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Compare and contrast how the relationship between technology and human connection is presented in the two texts. (Approximately 350 words) (20 marks)

Criterion A (Analysing) is worth 10 marks and Criterion B (Organizing) is worth 10 marks.
questions.mark_scheme: Total 20 marks: Criterion A (10) and Criterion B (10). Criterion A Analysing (10 marks). 0: no work that meets a descriptor. 1-2 (limited): identifies some content, language, structure or technique with few or no examples; little sense of how the texts relate. 3-4 (adequate): describes some features of the texts with some examples; a degree of understanding of how features create meaning; some awareness of similarity or difference. 5-6 (considerable): explains the effect of a range of features with relevant examples from both texts; clear understanding of how meaning is created; sound awareness of similarities and differences. 7-8 (substantial): analyses the effect of content, language, structure and technique in both texts with well-chosen evidence; thoughtful understanding of the writers' and creators' choices and of the relationship between the texts. 9-10 (excellent): perceptive, sustained analysis of both texts with precise, well-integrated evidence; insightful evaluation of how and why meaning is shaped, and a discerning view of the relationship between the texts. Indicative content for A (not exhaustive; credit any valid, evidenced point). Text A: technology as a seductive and isolating force; the endless scroll ('slid into the eleventh without his thumb ever deciding anything'), the personified screen that 'gave nothing back', the thumbs-up as a failed message, the contrast of the bin lorry and the peeling poster (the real world) with the phone; close third-person narration and the tentative ending in darkness that suggests possible change without resolving it. Text B: technology as a barrier that can be overcome by choice; the visual contrast of the muted crowd and the red kite; direct address, statistics, imperatives and a call to action; the tone moves from guilt to encouragement and practical hope ('No apps. Just people.'). Similarities: both show people physically near but emotionally apart; both use colour or light to separate the screen world from the real one; both suggest that real connection is within reach. Differences: private, ambiguous, internal in Text A versus public, persuasive and purposeful in Text B; Text A shows the problem through one character's story, Text B proposes a solution to a whole group; narrative withholds an answer, while the poster gives a clear one. Award up to [10] for Criterion A. Criterion B Organizing (10 marks). 0: no work that meets a descriptor. 1-2 (limited): little structure; the texts are mostly treated separately or in a list; ideas are hard to follow; little or no concluding thought. 3-4 (adequate): some structure with an opening and a close; both texts are discussed with a few links; some paragraphing and a degree of coherence. 5-6 (considerable): a clear structure; comparison and contrast appear in most paragraphs; ideas are generally logical and linked; an appropriate conclusion. 7-8 (substantial): an effective, purposeful structure; comparison and contrast are woven through the response; transitions are controlled and ideas build; a developed conclusion. 9-10 (excellent): a sophisticated, fully controlled structure that shapes the argument; comparison and contrast are integrated throughout; seamless linking; a conclusion that synthesizes the argument. Look for a comparative structure (for example by idea or by technique), topic sentences that name both texts, comparative connectives (whereas, similarly, in contrast) and a conclusion. Award up to [10] for Criterion B.

questions.content:
[[Q 2 | C 10 | D 10]]
Task 2: Producing literary text
This task focuses on the key concept of creativity. The criteria assessed are C (Producing text) and D (Using language). Suggested time: 35 minutes.

Image 1 (described in words): an old television set glows in a dark, empty living room. A single armchair is pulled close to it, a cup of tea steaming on its arm, and the screen shows only grey static that casts a flickering light on the wallpaper and a framed family photograph.
Image 2 (described in words): a girl stands alone on a flat city rooftop at dawn, holding a small handheld radio with its aerial raised towards a pale sky. Behind her, the lights of towers and windows are fading as the sun comes up.

Using one of the images, write a scene in a story in which a character hears or sees something that changes how they understand the world. You may consider purpose, characterisation, setting, mood and point of view. State which image you are using before you start. (Approximately 350 words) (20 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Total 20 marks: Criterion C (10) and Criterion D (10). Criterion C Producing text (10 marks). 0: no work that meets a descriptor. 1-2 (limited): limited creative choices; little imagination or insight; little detail; the image or prompt is hardly used. 3-4 (adequate): some creative choices; some imagination and insight; some relevant detail; the image and prompt are used in a basic way. 5-6 (considerable): thoughtful creative choices of content, character, setting and point of view; considerable imagination and insight; sufficient relevant detail. 7-8 (substantial): purposeful, imaginative choices; a developed voice and perspective; substantial insight; well-chosen detail that supports a clear purpose. 9-10 (excellent): highly original, perceptive choices; an assured, distinctive voice and perspective; extensive, precise detail and a controlled narrative or poetic shape that fully serves the prompt. A response that uses neither image and does not address the prompt scores 0 for Criterion C. Indicative content: the named image is clearly used as a starting point; a character with a clear motive; a controlled shift from not knowing to understanding; a purposeful setting and mood (for example anticipation, loneliness, wonder, unease); sensory detail, especially sound and light; a deliberate point of view; an ending that resonates. Credit science fiction, realist, mystery or poetic treatments. Award up to [10] for Criterion C. Criterion D Using language (10 marks). 0: no work that meets a descriptor. 1-2 (limited): limited range of vocabulary and structures; errors are frequent and often hinder communication; register is rarely appropriate. 3-4 (adequate): adequate range; a degree of accuracy; errors sometimes hinder communication; register is sometimes appropriate. 5-6 (considerable): a varied range of vocabulary, sentence structures and devices; considerable accuracy; errors do not hinder communication; register and style are generally appropriate. 7-8 (substantial): an effective range used with control; high accuracy with occasional slips; register and style are consistently appropriate and purposeful. 9-10 (excellent): a sophisticated, flexible range used with precision and flair; highly accurate with only minor errors; register and style are skilfully sustained throughout. Look for varied sentence length, precise verbs, controlled imagery and tense, and accurate punctuation. Award up to [10] for Criterion D.

questions.content:
[[Q 3 | B 10 | C 10 | D 10]]
Task 3: Producing non-literary text
This task focuses on the key concept of communication. You will create a piece of non-literary writing in relation to the global context scientific and technical innovation: digital life. The criteria assessed are B (Organizing), C (Producing text) and D (Using language). Suggested time: 50 minutes.

Your school is considering introducing a 'phone-free day' every week. Write a formal letter to the head teacher giving your view on this proposal and recommending what the school should do. Use a clear structure and the conventions of a formal letter, including an appropriate opening and close, a clear purpose, developed reasons supported by evidence and a persuasive but respectful tone. (Approximately 350 words) (30 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Total 30 marks: Criterion B (10), Criterion C (10) and Criterion D (10). Criterion B Organizing (10 marks). 0: no work that meets a descriptor. 1-2 (limited): little organisation; few or no text-type conventions; ideas not sequenced; paragraphing absent or random. 3-4 (adequate): some organisation; some conventions of the text type are used; a basic opening and ending; paragraphing is mostly logical. 5-6 (considerable): a clear structure; most conventions of the text type are used appropriately; ideas are generally sequenced and linked. 7-8 (substantial): an effective structure; conventions of the text type used purposefully; clear progression with controlled links and an effective opening and close. 9-10 (excellent): a skilfully crafted structure; conventions of the text type exploited for effect; seamless progression, with every paragraph contributing to the purpose and audience. Indicative content: sender and recipient details or an acceptable letter layout, date, formal salutation and sign-off that match (Dear Mr/Ms X ... Yours sincerely, or Dear Sir or Madam ... Yours faithfully), a subject line or an opening that states the purpose, logically sequenced paragraphs (position, reasons, counterargument, recommendation) and a courteous close. Award up to [10] for Criterion B. Criterion C Producing text (10 marks). 0: no work that meets a descriptor. 1-2 (limited): little insight into the global context or topic; little relevant detail; limited sense of audience and purpose. 3-4 (adequate): some insight into the global context; some relevant detail and examples; some awareness of audience and purpose. 5-6 (considerable): considerable insight into the global context and the topic; sufficient relevant detail and examples; a clear perspective and a good sense of audience and purpose. 7-8 (substantial): substantial, well-developed insight; well-chosen examples that support the argument; an assured perspective and a controlled appeal to the audience. 9-10 (excellent): perceptive, original insight into the global context; extensive, precise detail and examples; a distinctive, convincing perspective that fully serves the audience and purpose. Indicative content: insight into digital life, including benefits (research, communication, creativity, safety) and costs (distraction, sleep, wellbeing, comparison, reduced face-to-face contact); a clear and defensible position; specific evidence or examples from school life; consideration of the head teacher's concerns; a practical recommendation such as a trial period with review. Award up to [10] for Criterion C. Criterion D Using language (10 marks). 0: no work that meets a descriptor. 1-2 (limited): limited range of vocabulary and structures; errors are frequent and often hinder communication; register is rarely appropriate. 3-4 (adequate): adequate range; a degree of accuracy; errors sometimes hinder communication; register is sometimes appropriate. 5-6 (considerable): a varied range of vocabulary, sentence structures and devices; considerable accuracy; errors do not hinder communication; register and style are generally appropriate. 7-8 (substantial): an effective range used with control; high accuracy with occasional slips; register and style are consistently appropriate and purposeful. 9-10 (excellent): a sophisticated, flexible range used with precision and flair; highly accurate with only minor errors; register and style are skilfully sustained throughout. Look for a consistently formal register (no slang or contractions unless justified), measured persuasive devices, effective connectives and accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. Award up to [10] for Criterion D.
